body:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Asteria Head of ML), Daniel Park (Asteria Eng Lead), Rina Patel (Asteria Security)

Summary:
Customer evaluating migration from OpenAI-hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated (and possibility of private/VPC later). Primary drivers: cost predictability, latency tail, data residency/compliance. Wants parity in model outputs and low-friction migration (compatibility with existing prompt engineering, vLLM/TGI runtimes they use).

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, appreciate you carving time. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Liam, our SE. How are you all?
[00:07] Sofia: Good thanks, um we just — excited to learn, we've been running on OpenAI for prod and some Anthropic for safety checking, but costs are ballooning and latency spikes are painful.
[00:15] Daniel: Yep and the token costs, and the egress, and we need more control over fallback behavior when rate limits kick in.
[00:22] Liam: Totally, makes sense. Quick agenda — dig into current stack, constraints, eval parity questions, and then technical follow-ups like benchmarks and networking. Sound ok?
[00:30] Sofia: Yeah. Also want to confirm security posture — SOC2, encrypted logs, KMS.
[00:34] Rina: Right, SOC2 and SSO, plus we have to keep a record of audit trails for some customers.
[00:39] Maya: Great, we'll cover that and send the compliance pack afterwards.

[03:12] Daniel: Quick stack: we run inference through OpenAI API for chat completions and embeddings. For internal dev we sometimes run vLLM locally for iteration, and production has a mix — embeddings through OpenAI, gen through OpenAI's chat models. We use TGI for a few open models in staging.
[03:28] Liam: Got it. When you say vLLM locally, are you using it for latency comparisons or just for prototyping?
[03:33] Daniel: Both. We prototype on vLLM because it's cheap and replicable, but the production reliability isn't there so we piggyback on OpenAI.

[05:00] Sofia: Our main success criteria: 1) output parity — same quality as OpenAI for our prompt set, 2) latency P99 under 500ms for short-turn prompts (< 128 tokens), 3) cost per 1M tokens at least 30-40% better and predictable, 4) compliance (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS).
[05:20] Maya: That's helpful. On parity — we do model cataloging and can run side-by-side evals; we often find small prompt tweaks but you can pin models and we support canary rollouts.
[05:35] Liam: Also note that Redwood's runtime handles continuous batching and KV caching which helps with prefix heavy workloads. That usually improves p99 and reduces token spend.

[07:10] Daniel: How straightforward is it to keep the same prompt engineering? We have quite a few few-shot templates and tool-calling patterns.
[07:18] Liam: We'll probably see minimal changes. For function/tool calling we support structured outputs and streaming. Biggest differences are sometimes tokenization edge cases between model variants — we'll surface those in the eval.
[07:35] Sofia: We use tool-calls heavily — especially for retrieval augmentation and constraints.
[07:40] Maya: We can demo tool-calling parity in the pilot.

[10:05] Rina: On security, we need VPC peering or private connectivity, customer-managed keys, and audit logs retained for 12 months. Also SSO via SAML/Okta.
[10:15] Liam: Redwood Dedicated supports VPC and private control plane options; KMS integrations and HSM support for private deployments, audit logs are configurable. We'll share the security questionnaire and SOC2 artifacts.
[10:28] Rina: Do you have any customers with similar compliance needs?
[10:31] Maya: Yes, several enterprise healthcare and fintech customers on Dedicated/Private — we'll share case references.

[12:00] Daniel: Performance question — we run many short chat queries. Can Redwood hit p99 < 500ms? The p50 is fine, it's the tail that kills us.
[12:08] Liam: We have kernel-selection and runtime optimizations for autoregressive workloads; p99 is workload dependent (batching mix, seq length). For many customers we hit ~350-450ms p99 on Dedicated for short prompts with single-threaded connections and prefix caching. We'll need to run your traces.
[12:25] Sofia: Do you support vLLM/TGI model formats? We train some fine-tuned models in vLLM and also host TGI-based models in staging.
[12:33] Liam: We support major model formats and can load vLLM-flavored checkpoints; there may be conversion steps and quantization considerations. For TGI, if it's a pipeline that uses custom kernels, we'll validate compatibility — sometimes small ops differ. Part of the pilot is model onboarding and validating eval parity.

[15:45] Daniel: What's the pilot look like? We want to run our prompt set and compare outputs, latency, and token cost.
[15:52] Maya: Typical pilot: 2-4 week POC on Dedicated reserved slice or shared dev pool. We run your eval set, produce output diffs and regression metrics, and then a perf run with live-like traffic. We can provide a benchmark harness (Liam) to run both on your vLLM/TGI runner and on Redwood so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[16:12] Liam: We'll also suggest quantization profiles if cost is a concern; sometimes 4-bit quantization gives major cost wins with small quality tradeoffs. We'll surface quality metrics so you can decide.

[20:00] Sofia: About deterministic outputs — some of our safety checks rely on predictable sampling. Can you pin sampling params and seed behavior?
[20:07] Liam: You can pin temperature/top-p and we support deterministic sampling modes; seeding across different runtimes may still produce small variances but usually comparable. We'll include eval diffs to show variance.

[23:10] Rina: Network architecture — do you offer private endpoints inside our VPC or do we go over AWS peering?
[23:18] Liam: For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private link style arrangements; for Private (on-prem) we can run an air-gapped control plane. We'll get into specifics in the network deep-dive.

[27:45] Daniel: Billing model — we want predictable unit economics. How do reserved pools work versus hosted?
[27:53] Maya: Dedicated has reserved capacity contracts — you commit to a monthly GPU pool and get predictable throughput and lower per-token costs. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. There are also burst options for Dedicated if you need temporary extra capacity.

[30:00] Sofia: Any gotchas around embeddings? We currently use OpenAI embeddings for similarity. If we move embeddings to Redwood, will vector similarity results differ?
[30:10] Liam: Embeddings can differ by model; we have a catalog and recommended embeddings that match semantics of common OpenAI models. We'll run embedding parity tests as part of eval. If you need exact index compatibility, we can run side-by-side and surface drift metrics.

[33:40] Daniel: SLA and incident response?
[33:45] Maya: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and priority support options. We also have tracing and per-route dashboards in Redwood Console to help debug regressions.

[36:00] Sofia: Timeline: if we start pilot next week, what's a realistic path?
[36:07] Maya: If you share the prompt set and a lightweight spike dataset this week, Liam can spin a benchmark and we can have a 2-week eval running, with security docs in parallel — so 3-4 weeks to an initial decision.

[40:50] Rina: We'll need the security questionnaire filled for our procurement before PO.
[40:55] Maya: We'll prioritize that — you'll get SOC2 docs and the questionnaire back by Thursday.

[45:00] Maya: Recap — action items: we (Redwood) send pricing and reserved capacity options, Liam will share the benchmark harness and instructions, customer will provide prompt set and latency targets, and security will get SOC2 and questionnaire. Next meeting: network/VPC deep-dive with Rina on Aug 28.
[45:18] Sofia: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[45:24] Daniel: Thanks.
[45:27] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-attributions and small ASR errors on technical acronyms (TGI sometimes transcribed as 'T-G-I', vLLM as 'v L L M').

References shared during call: "Redwood Dedicated pricing deck" (link sent after), "Benchmark harness repo" (Liam to share), "Security questionnaire & SOC2" (Maya to send).
